text: Admin can upload a CSV file and map each column to a target - title, body, a custom field, or explicitly nothing.
A CSV import creates pages through the same path as any other creation, so slugging, validation and sanitisation apply unchanged.
A CSV import reports per row what was created, updated or skipped, naming the row number and the reason. A file mixing good and bad rows imports the good ones and leaves nothing half-written.
The import can target an existing website or create a new one, chosen on the first screen. Targeting an existing one needs an update-or-skip answer for every collision.
Admin can run the whole file through validation without writing anything, and see what would happen, before committing to it.
Columns are matched to fields automatically where the names correspond, ignoring case and accents; the admin can override every one of them.
Admin can download an example CSV generated from that website's own field definitions, with the right column headings already in it.
The mapping screen shows one real row from the file, navigable to the next, and each field can carry a default for cells that are empty or unmapped.

An uploaded CSV is treated as hostile: bytes, rows and single cells are all capped; a byte-order mark from Excel does not break the first column; a stray quote does not swallow the rest of the file; a short row is reported by its row number; a NUL byte is refused.
No transaction ever spans more than one row - the write pool admits a single connection, and a file-long transaction would block every other request on the machine.
